Forgotten figures

Helen Thompson Woolley and differences between the sexes

In 1903 she tested men and women and concluded they were far more alike than people believed.

In the late 19th century it was common to claim that women had less intellectual capacity than men, often with arguments about brain size. Helen Thompson Woolley (1874–1947) decided to test it.

More alike than different

For her thesis at the University of Chicago she assessed 25 male and 25 female students on tests of perception, memory, intelligence and emotion. She published the results in 1903 as The Mental Traits of Sex. The differences were small and the similarities much larger. And she attributed the differences she did find to upbringing and social environment, not biology.

She later worked in child psychology and in vocational guidance for young people. Her approach anticipated an idea modern research has confirmed: in most psychological abilities, men and women are much more alike than different.

References

  1. Thompson, H. B. (1903). The Mental Traits of Sex. University of Chicago Press.
  2. Hyde, J. S. (2005). The gender similarities hypothesis. American Psychologist, 60(6), 581–592.
